title: Why Contemporary Artists Can’t Stop Making Green Paintings
summary: The bartender looks up from making a drink, a lemon slice still held in hand, with an inscrutable expression, perhaps exhaustion, perhaps inviting. His hair, worn in two long braids, is a deep emerald hue, as is the long, billowy shirt he wears. A mirror positioned behind the bar reflects the night’s revelry in a dazzling array of perspectives, painted in verdant shades of green from mint to pine green, and passages of chartreuse. The painting, The Bar on East 13th (2019) by Salman Toor , is the centerpiece of “Someone Like You,” the New York painter’s first solo museum show in Europe, on view through January 10th at the Courtauld Gallery in London. The work is Toor’s reinterpretation of Édouard Manet ’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère (1882), itself part of the Courtauld’s permanent collection, and on view in an adjoining room. Whereas Manet’s 19th-century masterpiece was a study of light and reflection in blacks, grays, and whites, Toor’s vision is a heady, seductive vision in lush leafy greens. Over recent years, Toor’s works have become known for reveling in these verdant hues, and at the Courtauld show, about half of the 19 paintings of queer and immigrant life on view are dominated by them. “There’s something glamorous about emerald green—and something nocturnal, inviting,” Toor said of his fascination with the hue, which he first embraced around 2019. While Toor is perhaps the most well-known artist working with a green palette today, he is far from the only one. Contemporary artists including Brook Hsu , Colleen Barry , Jenny Morgan , and Huang Zhe are all embracing the color. Why? For these artists, and others, green, with its associations with nature as well as toxicity and the alien, is the nuanced color for our complex times. It embodies a collective longing for renewal Fugue, 2026 Colleen Barry Half Gallery Art historian and author Evie Hatch, who runs a popular Instagram account about pigment history, says the earliest known uses of green in art trace back to the use of malachite in ancient Egypt. While the hue has had varied meanings across cultures and times, “the association between green and fertility and growth is a recurring one,” she said in an interview. In ancient Egypt, artists often gave the god Osiris—god of agriculture, fertility, and the afterlife—green skin to link the renewal of vegetation to his resurrection, for instance. Hatch notes that green has more recently become the “color of ecological responsibility.” In June 1968, the Argentine artist Nicolás García Uriburu dyed Venice’s Grand Canal bright green with fluorescein during that year’s Biennale, to draw attention to pollution. Olafur Eliasson later paid tribute to the artwork with Green River (1998–2001), pouring harmless uranine into rivers in cities including Stockholm, Bremen, Los Angeles, and Tokyo. For contemporary artists, the embrace of green is less rooted in any sense of environmental advocacy than a desire for personal renewal and reconnection to the earth. New York artist Colleen Barry made her first predominantly green painting, The Feet Washers (2022), after years of painting in browns, earth tones, and dark backgrounds. “It reminds me of spring emerging from winter, when everything suddenly comes alive after months of gray and brown,” she said. Earlier this year, Barry opened “Iconophilia,” a solo exhibition at Half Gallery . Most of the works in the exhibition leaned into an emerald palette. For Barry, green reflects a cultural turn away from detachment and irony toward something more earnest. “Green is the color of life, growth, and regeneration,” Barry said, “so it makes sense that it would accompany this renewed interest in the human condition.” Green is also the color of poison and toxicity Cell Death 16, 2018 Brook Hsu Bahamas Biennale The Symbolizer, 2024 Jenny Morgan Anat Ebgi But green is far from purely positive. In the 19th century, the hue became associated with poison and toxicity. Scheele’s green, a warm yellowish leaf hue, was developed in the 1770s by Swedish German chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele and introduced commercially in 1814. The arsenic-based pigment was cheap and startlingly vivid. It was used to color candles, wallpaper, textiles, artificial flowers, and children’s toys. Yet, despite its widespread use, it was poisonous. Though most cases of arsenic poisoning were miserable but survivable, some were not. In 1861, Matilda Scheurer, a 19-year-old artificial flower maker in London, died of arsenic poisoning after dusting leaves with green powder. Her case was widely reported and helped turn public opinion against these pigments. These toxic associations for green still linger. “Poison is still so often drawn in lurid green,” said Hatch, noting scenes in popular culture, such as the poisoned apple dipped in green brew in Disney’s Snow White . Green embodies, in her words, “paradoxical associations—with growth and renewal, and sickness and poison.” Last year, artist Maja Ruznic made an installation of paintings for the SITE Santa Fe International which centered around the color green. For Ruznic, who was born in Bosnia and lives in New Mexico, green became a subconscious way of referencing both the green fields of her homeland and the state’s history as a nuclear testing ground and, infamously, the site of Area 51. “I think about the land as being both beautiful but also still radioactive,” she said at the time . Other lasting associations with the color green, as both glamorous and hallucinatory, may have been introduced by the popularity of absinthe, a green liquor popular during the late 19th century. Absinthe was fashionably consumed at the l’heure verte ( or the green hour), a five o’clock feature at cafés in Paris and Prague. The drink was popular with artists including Van Gogh and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec , and became associated (on poor evidence) with hallucination and madness. The green glow of absinthe is a direct inspiration for Toor’s green paints as well as the jewel tones of emeralds and jade. New York and Wyoming–based painter Brook Hsu is known for her often mythic, sometimes autobiographical small-scale paintings rendered in hues of green, currently on view in the show “Trout Fishing in America” at Heidi in London. Hsu’s interest in the color is complex, but relates originally to the body and illness. About a decade ago, she saw someone vomit the “softest pale green-blue” and her relationship to the color changed. “The experience awakened me, and I fell in love,” she said in an interview. She thinks of herself as being in an ongoing relationship with the color, she added, and described her work with green as “intimate.” For others, green simply offers a sense of distance Control, 2025 Huang Zhe 黄喆 AAIE Gallery Green smoke, 2025 Huang Zhe 黄喆 AAIE Gallery For some artists, the color reflects the passage of time, the unreality of a dream state, or simply a critical distance from the demands of the moment. New York artist Jenny Morgan moved toward a cooler palette around 2016 and was deeply engaged with painting in minty tones by 2019, moving from skin tones to bodies and surroundings painted fully green. “Green felt like an immediate escape hatch out of the body,” she said, a move away from the warm and knowable toward something alien. She reads the wider trend of artists leaning into greens as a sign of a communal desire to escape, whether into nature, away from the body, or into a shared alternate space. For Florence-based artist Huang Zhe, green is the color of memory. He grew up in a Buddhist family in southern China, where ceremonies and folk rituals were red, the color of good fortune. After more than a decade away, studying in Beijing and then Italy, “the red of my hometown gradually faded into yellow, and then into green in my memory.” Green became a way of filtering perception and emotion, he added, first carrying estrangement and later, as his work developed, associations with nature and vitality. Barry sees green similarly, saying that in her figurative paintings, green can make an image feel “both intensely alive and strangely distant, like in a memory.” Huang, for his part, sees artists embracing green palettes as a resistance to immediate legibility, a muddling of emotional meanings. “It can introduce distance and uncertainty, inviting a slower and more contemplative way of looking.” Green, in his reading, lets feelings stay unresolved. But perhaps this penchant for green will only be understood in time. Art, as Barry said, “often reveals the psychological needs of its time before we can fully articulate them.” Browse more green artworks in Artsy's collection.

title: India Art Fair announces more than 120 exhibitors for 2027 edition.
summary: India Art Fair will return for its 18th edition at the NSIC Exhibition Grounds in New Delhi from February 4th through 7th, 2027, with more than 120 exhibitors spanning galleries, institutions, and design practices from India and abroad Returning international galleries include David Zwirner , Galleria Continua , neugerriemschneider, Carpenters , Whitestone Gallery , and Sundaram Tagore Gallery , alongside new exhibitors including London’s Chilli (London) and Opera Gallery , which has 16 locations worldwide. Leading Indian galleries also feature prominently, including Nature Morte , Vadehra Art Gallery , Chemould Prescott Road, Jhaveri Contemporary , Experimenter, and DAG . Three Delhi galleries—Gallery Vayu, Gallery XXL, and Pristine Contemporary —will also be joining for the first time. The 18th edition of India Art Fair reflects the remarkable energy and ambition of South Asia’s artistic landscape today," said fair director Jaya Asokan. “What makes our 2027 fair particularly exciting is the momentum we have built through our year-round programming across the country.” The fair’s Focus section will present solo presentations by artists including Rina Banerjee with Vadehra Art Gallery, Sameer Kulavoor with TARQ, and Ketaki Sarpotdar with LATITUDE 28, while its Platform section continues to spotlight South Asia’s craft and Indigenous artistic traditions, including a Tantric art survey from the Crites Collection and ICA Gallery. Contemporary artist Jitish Kallat will reimagine the fair’s façade with a new architectural iteration of his work Here After Here After Here , rendering a network of highway signage across its exterior. “A highway sign stands here but is always about elsewhere,” Kallat said. “On the façade, the immediate becomes entangled with distant geographies and other times, as well as with places that live in myth.” Outdoor art projects elsewhere on the fairgrounds will include a large-scale installation by Birender Yadav presented by the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art and Time, Cosmos, and the City , a textile and graphic installation by December Design marking three centuries since Jaipur’s founding, presented by the City Palace Museum. The fair will also mark the sixth edition of its BMW India-backed Future Is Born of Art Commission, which invites an artist to transform a space at the fair into a digital exploration of imagination and technology. “As BMW Group India marks its 11th year of partnership with India Art Fair, we reaffirm our commitment to giving artists the freedom to explore, experiment, and bring bold ideas to life,” said Hardeep Singh Brar, president and CEO of BMW Group India.

title: 5 Artists on our Radar in October 2026
summary: Inflorescência, 2026 Thalita Hamaoui Simões de Assis “Artists on Our Radar” is a monthly series focused on five artists who have our attention. Utilizing our art expertise and Artsy data, we’ve determined which artists made an impact this past month through new gallery representation, exhibitions, auctions, art fairs, or fresh works on Artsy. James Owens B. 1995, Middlesbrough, U.K. Lives and works in London. Night in the Woods, 2020 James Owens PM/AM I Don’t Like a Bank That Hides Its Skeletons, 2026 James Owens Public Gallery British painter James Owens conjures imagined scenes that are shaped by his childhood spent between the countryside and a Yorkshire fishing village. In Owens’s Symbolist -like paintings, sunflowers sway ominously and grass blades droop under beads of water. His figures are often overlaid with patterns and abstractions, so that they seem to recede into their surroundings in a kind of camouflage. Owens was part of Artsy’s emerging art fair Foundations in 2024 and exhibited works at Kiaf SEOUL 2024 . Earlier this month, Newchild Gallery announced his representation, and this November, Owens will be featured at the gallery in an upcoming duo exhibition with Yoo Geun-Taek . Thalita Hamaoui B. 1981, São Paulo. Lives and works in São Paulo. Fim do horizonte, 2026 Thalita Hamaoui Simões de Assis Ritmo da terra, 2026 Thalita Hamaoui Simões de Assis Brazilian artist Thalita Hamaoui paints large, colorful landscapes built from memory and family storytelling. In a recent series, she painted scenery drawn from stories her grandmother told about her native Romania—a country Hamaoui has never visited. Filtered through the tropical environment she knows, the hills, seas, and flowering plants take on a lush look. Folklore, fantasy, and grief over her grandmother’s death run through the work, and the ground often seems to give way even as the terrain becomes a refuge, a place of possibility. Hamaoui cites Brazilian Tropicália, a counterculture movement of the 1960s, along with Impressionists such as Pierre Bonnard as her influences. She studied fine art at Fundação Armando Alvares Penteado and spent years working in textile printing, an experience that continues to influence her understanding of form and color. Hamaoui’s works were recently presented alongside historic works by Brazilian modern artist Miguel Bakun at a duo booth with Simões de Assis at Frieze London . Her New York solo debut, “Nascer da Terra,” was at Marianne Boesky. Earlier this spring she opened “ Corpo de Vento ” at Simões de Assis . Qian Zhong B. 1995, Sichuan, China. Lives and works in London. Afterimage, 2026 Qian Zhong Soho Revue Artist Qian Zhong paints surreal , fragmented figures that explore women’s identity and desire. In her current solo show “ Almost Body ” on view at Soho Revue in London through October 31st, cropped-in snapshots of feminine bodies—an abdomen, a lower back, a crotch—are shown tightly clad in shiny lamé and sequined dresses. These spectacle-like ensembles offer a juxtaposition to the introspective, even lonely quality of the works, like coming home after a long night or standing alone on a crowded dance floor. Zhong, who was born in Sichuan, earned her MA in painting at the Royal College of Art in London in 2025. Before that, she founded a studio in Chengdu, China, focused on public and community-based art, and her experience with large-scale murals informs how she handles space and visual impact on canvas. Alejandro Javaloyas B. 1987, Palma de Mallorca, Spain. Lives and works in Toulouse, France. Is there a murder in your film?, 2025 Alejandro Javaloyas Galeria Reus Neither shall ye profane my holy name (Leviticus 22:32), 2026 Alejandro Javaloyas Galeria Reus Toulouse-based artist Alejandro Javaloyas creates intimately scaled, hazy, atmospheric images that balance a delicacy of form and color with a foreboding sense of unease. This summer, Javaloyas’s solo exhibition “Un cuchillo que no corta” at Galeria Reus in Palma, Spain, delved deep into this tension. The book-size paintings were inspired by recurring nightmares the artist has, which he logs in a dream journal he has kept for years. Javaloyas then uses AI models to visualize his notes, selects a few images from many variations, and reworks them digitally into prints. The prints, made on cotton paper and layered with wax-based colored pencil, show burning houses, crashed cars, and baby teeth with the blur of a dream. Javaloyas holds a master’s degree in film from ESCAC Barcelona Film School at the University of Barcelona, and many of his influences are cinematic, including directors such as Andrei Tarkovsky, Chris Marker , and David Lynch . This year, he won the 20th edition of the Prisma Art Prize with his colored pencil diptych titled Incredulità di San Tommaso (2026) . Austin Hayman B. 1989, Santa Monica, California. Lives and works in Los Angeles. Looking for a Friend, 2026 Austin Hayman Make Room Los Angeles painter Austin Hayman makes figurative oil paintings that teeter on the edge of Surrealism . Simple domestic scenes—girls braiding each other’s hair, for instance—are made unfamiliar by the introduction of out-of-place elements like a single green apple or a glowing candle that create a Magritte -like effect. These figures are usually people Hayman knows in spaces they inhabit. A self-taught painter, Hayman has recently been on the rise. This summer, he had a solo show, “Looking for a Friend,” at Make Room in Los Angeles. Other recent exhibitions include the solo show “Won’t Say Anything at All” at Allgorithm Gallery in Los Angeles and the group exhibition “Inherent Manifest” at Gambit Gallery in New York.

title: The 5 Best Booths at Artissima 2026
summary: Autumn is a fine time to be an art lover in Turin. With golden foliage lining the city’s grand boulevards and Piedmontese white truffle season in full swing, the city was looking its best as visitors arrived under clear blue skies for the VIP preview of Artissima 2026 on October 29th. Artissima takes place right in the thick of Europe’s bustling fall art calendar, arriving hot on the heels of Frieze London and Art Basel Paris . But the Turin fair is no newcomer. Founded in 1994, it predates both of its heavyweight counterparts and has spent more than three decades carving out a distinctive identity. Now on its 33rd edition, the fair brings together 183 galleries from 35 countries at the Oval Lingotto Fiere. Unlike its larger European counterparts, Artissima isn’t primarily a destination for blue-chip blockbusters. Rather, it’s a hub for experimentation, with adventurous presentations, emerging artists, and younger galleries taking center stage. For collectors, that means a chance to encounter unfamiliar names and acquire works by promising artists early in their careers. It’s also a favorite among curators and museum directors, who come to scout talent and forge relationships that can lead to institutional opportunities for artists. “More than ever this year, we try to highlight how Artissima is a fair of discoveries,” director Luigi Fassi told Artsy ahead of the opening. For him, this means “galleries and artists that even well-traveled collectors are not familiar with.” A longtime champion of the fair is collector and philanthropist Patrizia Sandretto Re Rebaudengo . She pointed to the fair’s growing international network, including a group of collectors visiting from China, and its enduring commitment to emerging talent. “Even 25 years ago, it was a fair like it is now, a fair in which you could find a new gallery, new energy, new discovery,” she said. That spirit of exploration is supported by a substantial institutional network, including a new Curators’ Choice initiative involving 18 European curators, and a €300,000 ($334,872) acquisition fund supporting works for Turin’s museums. This year, the fair makes its case for experimentation with installations that melt, artworks that demand physical interaction, and unconventional presentations. Here are five booths that stood out. Night Café Booth New Entries 1 With works by Mandy Franca Sweeping across the walls of Night Café ’s booth , dramatic images of orange clouds against dark skies are printed onto lengths of fabric that hang, fold, and spill towards the floor. This installation, from Dutch artist Mandy Franca , brings together works from her ongoing series “In a State of Being,” its first solo outing in Italy. Rather than conventional photographs, the works are layered collages assembled from Franca’s personal archive of images, many of which were taken on her phone. She prints them onto materials including satin silk and voile, then reworks them with oil pastels and other media, turning them into sculptural objects. The fabric’s folds and creases disrupt the original compositions. In In a State of Being IV (2026), for instance, fiery orange clouds stretch across overlapping panels of dark fabric, creating an uneasy sense of movement and impending change. In a State of Being V, 2026 Mandy Franca Night Café In a State of Being IV, 2026 Mandy Franca Night Café In a State of Being II, 2021 Mandy Franca Night Café In a State of Being I, 2021 Mandy Franca Night Café Untitled, 2025 Mandy Franca Night Café “This body of work is really about mark-making and thinking about all of the traces that we leave behind,” gallery founder Maribelle Bierens told Artsy. Clouds are a recurring motif in Franca’s practice, which Bierens described as “a symbol of freedom,” noting that while they appear to move freely, “there are a lot of invisible forces that shape” them. The works also reference climate change, Bierens noted: The orange skies reference ominous and extreme changes in the weather. Prices range from €4,500 ($5,000) to €15,000 ($16,700). LOHAUS Gallery Booth Orange 12 With works by Melanie Siegel and Sarah Zagefka Empty swimming pools, deserted tennis courts, and modest shopfronts take center stage at LOHAUS Gallery ’s two-person presentation, “ The Presence of Absence .” Bringing together paintings by Melanie Siegel and Sarah Zagefka , the Munich-based gallery explores the traces that people leave behind in their surroundings, even when no figures are in sight. Siegel’s paintings depict carefully ordered environments in which nature and architecture coexist uneasily. In Window (I) (2026), a turbulent sea is seen through a window from the safety of a warm interior. What appear to be birds flying across the storm outside are actually silhouettes stuck to the pane of glass, complicating the view. Gehäuse (V), 2026 Melanie Siegel LOHAUS GALLERY Window (I), 2026 Melanie Siegel LOHAUS GALLERY Window (II), 2026 Melanie Siegel LOHAUS GALLERY Gehäuse (VI), 2026 Melanie Siegel LOHAUS GALLERY w.22-5, 2026 Sarah Zagefka LOHAUS GALLERY TS.330-6, 2026 Sarah Zagefka LOHAUS GALLERY AQ.19-3, 2026 Sarah Zagefka LOHAUS GALLERY CT.82-7, 2026 Sarah Zagefka LOHAUS GALLERY AH.24-5, 2026 Sarah Zagefka LOHAUS GALLERY K.H.23-8, 2026 Sarah Zagefka LOHAUS GALLERY TS.330-6, 2026 Sarah Zagefka LOHAUS GALLERY Zagefka, meanwhile, finds intrigue in the streets. Her small, meticulously rendered paintings capture shopfronts and overlooked corners encountered during travels through Jordan, Italy, and Germany. Among them is AQ.19-3 (2026), an intimate oil-on-wood painting from her travels in the Middle East. “If you look at something and it’s not that spectacular, and you look at it longer, it gets more interesting,” the artist told Artsy. “The longer you look, the more you understand why it looks like it looks.” Working in oil over charcoal sketches, often on wooden supports she constructs herself, these small, intricate paintings record the details that give everyday places their character. Bremond Capela Booth Green 14 With works by Louise Vo Tan and Valdrin Thaqi At Bremond Capela ’s booth, visitors must crouch to appreciate the art. Arranged in three neat rows across the floor, 15 weathered metal boxes invite curious fairgoers to bend down and peer inside, as many were spotted doing during the opening preview. Each contains a channel of French Vietnamese artist Louise Vo Tan’s multimedia installation Pendant que les champs brûlent (2026). These small video screens play archival footage of the European Parliament and Banque de France. Some of the recordings feed into soundscapes composed by the artist, who also works as a DJ. Also in the boxes are scattered photographic fragments, and a partially burned family portrait, its charred edges framing a surviving face. It’s a reference to a recent disaster: A fire destroyed Vo Tan’s family home and much of its photographic archive. “She managed to save some,” gallery co-founder Mathieu Capela told Artsy, explaining how the artist combines these surviving images with film and sound gathered from bureaucratic centers of power “not accessible to everyone.” By bringing these materials together, Vo Tan contrasts the fragility of personal memory with the authority of institutions that shape and preserve official histories. On the surrounding walls are quiet paintings by Kosovo-based artist Valdrin Thaqi . Shaped in soft, muted tones with delicate brushwork, the carefully composed scenes have an almost photographic stillness. Two large canvases depict the same woman in a long white dress, first covering part of her face with one hand, then concealing it entirely with both. Her gestures are simple but ambiguous, leaving viewers to do the contextual guesswork. “With one element, [he] makes you wonder what happened before or what will happen after,” Capela explained. Together, the works explore what images reveal, conceal, and preserve. Prices for Thaqi’s paintings range from €5,000 ($5,500) to €18,000 ($20,150), while Vo Tan’s complete installation is priced at €12,000 ($13,400). Secci Booth PF3 With works by Emma Scarafiotti With its pastel-pink walls and pale carpet, Secci ’s booth drew many curious visitors during the VIP preview, its inviting appearance contrasting with the occasionally unsettling works of Italian artist Emma Scarafiotti . The solo presentation spans video, photography, AI-assisted imagery, and performance, exploring bodies that twist, merge, and transform. Among the highlights are XRay FULL BODY UNKNOWN 01 and XRay HALF BODY UNKNOWN 01 (both 2026), elongated lightboxes each displaying six stills from the artist’s videos. In muted pinks and browns, the images resemble microscopic studies of skin and tissue. “You see something that is unknown, like different parts together,” a gallery representative told Artsy, describing Scarafiotti’s interest in “the mutation of the body.” Baccanti, 2025 Emma Scarafiotti Secci AI-QUARIUM,, 2026 Emma Scarafiotti Secci XRay FULL BODY UNKNOWN 01, 2026 Emma Scarafiotti Secci XRay HALF BODY UNKNOWN 01, 2026 Emma Scarafiotti Secci Nearby, a glossy lilac-framed monitor displays an ever-morphing AI-generated form, at times resembling a spiny seashell or marine creature. “You never see the same,” the representative explained. At the back, Baccanti (2025), a three-act film inspired by the female followers of Dionysus in ancient Greece, shows bodies intertwining and merging into unfamiliar shapes, exploring collective movement and fluid identities. Finally, in the corner lies a crumpled white costume, detached sleeves, and scattered locks of dark hair awaiting the artist’s live performance, scheduled for Saturday. These theatrical elements reflect Scarafiotti’s wider practice, which combines filmmaking, collaborations with dancers, and digital technologies to explore queer identity and the shifting boundaries between human and nonhuman life. Prices for works range from €6,500 ($7,200) to €8,500 ($9,500). Matèria Booth Red 10 With works by Stefano Canto, José Angelino, and Mario Cresci Artworks don’t often melt before your eyes, but that’s precisely what’s happening at Matèria ’s booth . At its center, Stefano Canto has assembled a makeshift construction site of terra-cotta bricks, cement bags, and concrete blocks, topped with two pigment-colored ice sculptures resembling human heads. As the ice melts, water seeps into the cement powder beneath, causing it to harden and preserve the impressions left by the disappearing forms. Works made from a similar process, including SP5 (2026), hang on the surrounding walls, their colorful, layered surfaces resembling weathered fossils. “It’s a rush against time,” gallery manager Rossana Esposito told Artsy, describing a process that is carefully planned yet ultimately unpredictable. This fascination with transformation is also visible in José Angelino ’s delicate glass sculptures, which use electricity and gases to generate glowing, shifting colors. In Orbitali 01 (2018), tubes of blown glass filled with argon gas produce an ethereal light, inspired by the atmospheric phenomena behind the Northern Lights. Drawing on his background in physics, Angelino explores the unpredictable interactions between energy and matter. Anamorfosi, Venezia, 1967, 2026 Mario Cresci Matèria Anamorfosi, Venezia, 1967, 2026 Mario Cresci Matèria Pinocchio Narciso, Matera 1990 (Set of 9 works), 1990 Mario Cresci Matèria SP7, 2026 Stefano Canto Matèria SP5, 2026 Stefano Canto Matèria SP14, 2026 Stefano Canto Matèria SP15, 2026 Stefano Canto Matèria SP13, 2026 Stefano Canto Matèria SP21, 2026 Stefano Canto Matèria SP 20, 2026 Stefano Canto Matèria SP 22, 2026 Stefano Canto Matèria Cloacina #1, 2026 Stefano Canto Matèria SP00, 2017 Stefano Canto Matèria Senza titolo (Untitled), 2026 José Angelino Matèria Orbitali 01, 2018 José Angelino Matèria A different kind of experimentation appears in Mario Cresci ’s pair of abstract photographic compositions that stretch and distort images into unfamiliar forms. They’re from the artist’s 1967 heliographic prints, revisited as limited-edition photographic works and conceived to preserve the fragile 1967 experimentations while making the seminal series accessible to a wider audience. The newly printed works reflect his longstanding interest in photography’s ability to transform reality rather than just record it. Together, the works make for an intriguing exploration of physical processes. Prices range from approximately €3,000 ($3,300) to €35,000 ($39,100).

title: Centre Pompidou, MoMA, and M+ form new cultural alliance.
summary: Centre Pompidou , MoMA , and M+ have formed a new cultural alliance, the three institutions announced Friday. The museums have agreed to share their collections with one another's audiences, co-organize exhibitions and programs, and deepen their joint curatorial research and conservation work. The museum directors—Christophe Cherix of MoMA, Laurent Le Bon of Centre Pompidou, and Suhanya Raffel of M+—signed a framework agreement at an event at M+ in Hong Kong. Each museum will retain its independence and identity, but the alliance is intended to give their combined 10 million annual in-person visitors and 125 million online visitors expanded access . Founded in 1929, 1977, and 2021 respectively, MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ each represented a new model for collecting institutions focused on the art of their time. Together the museums hold a broad, multidisciplinary record of 20th- and 21st-century creativity across three continents. “This cultural alliance makes our museums embassies for each other, in effect creating an extraordinary gateway that opens onto three continents,” MoMA’s Cherix said. “Beyond expanding our reach to an unprecedented level, the cultural alliance also deepens intellectual exchange, as we align our programming, organize joint exhibitions, preserve art, and unite audiences worldwide, allowing us to function as more than the sum of our parts.” “No single institution can encompass the entire scope of global creativity. We aim to work on a broader and deeper level,” said Pompidou’s Le Bon, adding that the alliance would “enable long-term loans, deepening the presentation of key artists and movements.” The alliance arrives as Centre Pompidou marks its 50th anniversary with “Constellation,” a year of exhibitions and programs in Paris and internationally, while its landmark Beaubourg building undergoes an extensive renovation. M+’s Raffel, meanwhile, framed the partnership as a chance to widen whose perspectives shape the story of modern and contemporary art. “As Asia's global museum of contemporary visual culture, M+ brings perspectives from Hong Kong and our region to this dialogue,” Raffel said “We hope to create new opportunities for artists and audiences, shape a more cooperative and sustainable future for museums, and reimagine how cultural narratives resonate around the world.”

title: How This Painting of Witches Became a Metaphor for Female Political Power
summary: Clouds whirl across the night sky, only a sliver of moon visible. In these woods, three witches are gathered around a cauldron. An orange cat and a ram cavort beside them, and a ghoulish face emerges from the darkness. But the witches themselves are anything but frightening. No crones with warts and knobby fingers, these ladies are the epitome of elegance, wearing diaphanous gowns and stupendous hats that cascade with long veils. Youthful, with porcelain skin and rosy cheeks, they strike refined poses. One witch on the right, wearing a pointy black hat, looks out from the artwork toward the viewer, aware she is being watched. The Three Witches from Macbeth (1775), by the British portraitist Daniel Gardner, is now in the collection of London’s National Portrait Gallery . Every year, as Halloween approaches, the museum tends to highlight the spooky but spectacular gouache-and-chalk painting. Gardner was a well-known society portraitist and a student of the fashionable painter George Romney , from whom, he famously claimed, he learned little. His witches aren’t fantastical: His models were three of the most influential women in Georgian England. This triple portrait captures Elizabeth Lamb, Viscountess Melbourne (left); Georgiana Cavendish, Duchess of Devonshire (center); and the sculptor Anne Seymour Damer (right) decked out as the three witches of Shakespeare’s Macbeth . In the play, the trio prophesy Macbeth’s rise to the kingship and ultimately lead him to his demise. Society women were sometimes portrayed as classical or pastoral figures, but depicting three women as characters in a theatrical scene was unusual. The painting is a quizzical outlier in Gardner’s oeuvre—the only time he depicted his sitters in costume—yet it reflects a larger fascination with gothic and supernatural themes that took place in Georgian England. The late 1700s saw a widespread fascination with Macbeth In the mid-to-late 1700s, a Macbeth mania swept through English public culture. For well over a century, the play had been out of style. English theaters had been shuttered from 1642 to 1660 by order of the Puritan government. For close to 100 years after they reopened, Macbeth was performed only rarely. That changed in 1744, when the actor and writer David Garrick debuted a new production of Macbeth that returned more faithfully to Shakespeare’s text, bringing the play back into the limelight. The three witches became a popular motif in art and poetry, with artists including Henry Fuseli , William Blake , and Romney all painting or drawing their own versions of Macbeth ’s three witches. The public fascination with Macbeth and its famous king-killing may have been stirred, in part, by the discord in nearby France, which crescendoed from the protests and riots of the 1760s and ’70s to the bloody tumult of the revolution itself in the final years of the century. At the same time England was under the rule of King George III, the so-called “mad king,” who was known for mental health episodes that might have seemed not dissimilar to Macbeth’s outbursts. Amid heavy censorship of the era, Shakespeare’s play offered an outlet for contemporary anxieties. The portrait celebrates three patrons of the arts Lady Melbourne, the Duchess of Devonshire, and Anne Seymour Damer were high-powered friends and well-known supporters of the theater. All three women took part in amateur productions at the private theater at Althorp, the Duchess of Devonshire’s family estate. Lady Melbourne is thought to have commissioned the portrait from Gardner, and it descended through her family. Scholars believe either she or Damer may have suggested the composition. A plaster portrait bust of Lord Nelson after Anne Seymour Damer, ca. 1802 A plaster portrait bust of Lord Nelson after Anne Seymour Damer Wick Antiques Ltd Damer was also a well-known sculptor of the era. Encouraged by her guardian Horace Walpole, she studied different types of art with a number of prominent teachers of the era, including modeling with Giuseppe Ceracchi, marble carving with John Bacon , and anatomy with William Cumberland Cruikshank. She worked chiefly in the Neoclassical style, making busts that moved from early wax pieces to technically complex work in terra-cotta, bronze, and marble. Her subjects were largely her society friends, like politician Charles James Fox and, later, British naval admiral Horatio Nelson . She also portrayed the actresses Sarah Siddons (who earned fame for her turn as Lady Macbeth in the 1780s) and Elizabeth Farren (a popular comic performer) as Muses. Her art often referenced the world of theater. For instance, she made a statue of Apollo for the façade of Drury Lane Theatre and a bas-relief for the Boydell Shakespeare Gallery. Gardner’s portrait was also one of political power By the time of this portrait, all three women held prominent positions in British society and shared a passion for Whig politics. Lady Melbourne had been friends with Damer since the early 1770s, while her friendship with the Duchess of Devonshire was newer. The portrait may in part reflect Lady Melbourne’s wish to publicize that new intimacy with the Duchess, who would go on to host England’s most influential political salon from 1776. The National Portrait Gallery describes Gardner’s choice of the cauldron scene to represent their “shadowy political machinations” as leading members of the Devonshire House circle. The witches in the play, after all, famously urge Macbeth toward power. The painting is not known to have been exhibited in its time, but contemporaries clearly knew of it. Lady Mary Coke wrote in her 1775 journal of “the Duchess of Devonshire, Lady Melburn, and Mrs Damer all being drawn in one picture in the Characters of the three Witches in Macbeth…They have chosen that Scene where they compose their Cauldron, but instead of ‘finger of Birth-strangled babe, etc’ their Cauldron is composed of roses and carnations and I daresay they think their charmes more irresistible than all the magick of the Witches.” The label of “witch” has historically been used to discredit women whose power made others uneasy. By casting themselves in the role, with roses in place of grisly ingredients, these three society women seem to claim power for themselves, treating the idea of dangerous female influence as a compliment rather than an insult. title: Artist Prince Gyasi and singer Davido collaborate on limited-edition Martell cognac bottle.
summary: Artist Prince Gyasi and singer Davido have collaborated on a limited-edition Martell cognac bottle. Maison Martell unveiled its Martell Afrobeats collection this week in New York, marking the global launch of the new Martell VS and XO limited-edition bottle designs. The release builds on Martell’s five-year relationship with Davido and introduces Gyasi’s new role as the Maison's creative partner. For the Martell VS label, Gyasi reworked Davido’s portrait in his signature saturated, block-color style, surrounding it with soundwaves meant to evoke the singer's global reach, while incorporating Martell’s house blue branding alongside gold and wave-like forms inspired by the landscapes of West Africa. An XO expression, designed separately, will launch exclusively in Africa. “When I hear music, I experience it visually,” Gyasi said in a statement. “With these designs, I wanted to capture the feeling of Afrobeats—the movement, the joy, the confidence, and the way it connects people across the world. Davido brings that energy through music, and I wanted to translate it through color, movement, and emotion.” Davido, for his part, framed the bottle as a natural extension of his partnership with the brand: “Five years with Martell, and we’ve built something really special for this launch. Bringing Prince into the mix to connect the music with his creative vision took it to a new level.” Gyasi, who is self-taught and took up photography as a teenager in Accra using an iPhone, is known for surreal compositions informed by his synesthesia, which links colors to words and emotions. He became the first African artist to shoot the Pirelli Calendar, creative-directing its 50th-anniversary 2024 edition. He was also named one of Time’ s Next Generation Leaders in 2023, and has collaborated with Apple, Off-White, and Balmain. His work is held in the Pinault Collection, the Jean Pigozzi Collection, and the Museu de Arte do Rio . Davido, the most-followed Afrobeats artist on social media, released his sixth studio album, ORIADÉ , this summer. The New York launch, hosted by Martell culture ambassador Adesope “Shopsydoo” Olajide, included a fireside conversation between Davido and Gyasi and closed with a live Davido performance. The announcement coincides with the release of Davido's new music video for “Already Falling,” filmed at Martell’s historic Château de Chanteloup estate in Cognac, France, and featuring the new bottle designs. “Martell’s heritage is rooted in craftsmanship and an optimistic spirit, with an openness to the cultural forces shaping our world,” said Sébastien Borda, Pernod Ricard’s vice president of marketing for prestige brands. “Through this limited edition, Davido and Prince Gyasi bring music, art, and design together in a way that feels distinctive, joyful, and contemporary.” The Martell VS Afrobeats bottle is available now at retailers across the U.S. and on Martell.com for $35, while supplies last. The XO limited-edition bottle will roll out separately in Nigeria, Ghana, and Kenya.

title: Late Artist Teruko Yokoi’s Blooming Abstractions Are Capturing New Attention
summary: Untitled, 2000 Teruko Yokoi Hollis Taggart Luminous fields of color and loose brushstrokes fill the abstract compositions of Teruko Yokoi . In Untitled (2000), green clouds sit against an ethereal purple background, like trees hovering above a field caught in the light of a sunset. For Yokoi, a landscape could capture memories and fleeting moments of time. The Japan-born artist, who spent formative years in San Francisco and New York before settling in Switzerland, developed a distinctive visual language that united post-war abstraction with the rhythms of traditional Japanese painting. Although Yokoi, who died in 2020 at the age of 96, exhibited widely during her lifetime, including at San Francisco’s Palace of the Legion of Honor, her position within post-war abstraction still deserves reconsideration. Though she was married to Abstract Expressionist star Sam Francis , her name has faded in comparison to his. “Her career followed an asymmetrical trajectory, shaped by circumstances that led her to leave the United States just as her career was gaining global attention,” the artist’s grandson and managing director of Yokoi's estate, Tai Francis Wallace, told Artsy. “I think her relative absence from the broader American art historical narrative reflects the challenges faced by women artists of her generation.” This fall, with exhibitions at James Fuentes Gallery in Los Angeles (through November 7th) and Hollis Taggart in New York (through November 25th), Yokoi is finally earning her due regard. Yokoi’s early life Born in 1924 in Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Yokoi was introduced to painting and poetry by her father. “As a little girl, Teruko would accompany her father, a calligrapher, on walks through the countryside to ‘haiku hiroi’ [collect haiku], drawing inspiration from nature for poetry,” Yokoi’s daughter, Kayo Malik and a custodian of her estate, told Artsy. “During her teenage years, she contemplated whether to become an artist or a poet, ultimately realizing that she could paint her poems in colors rather than words.” Indeed, Yokoi often called her paintings “poems written in colors,” a description that captures their balance of immediacy and restraint. From her early days spending time outside with her father, the natural world became an enduring subject for the artist. Yokoi’s work is at once expansive and intimate, its fields of color and abbreviated brushstrokes evoking the fleeting impressions of blossoms, foliage, snow, and changing light. “Growing up in Japan during World War II and coming of age in its aftermath gave her an understanding of the natural world as something continually shifting around her,” said Wallace. “Her work invites us to pay closer attention to those fleeting moments of beauty, stillness, and passing seasons. There is something very universal in the memories and the emotions you experience when you stand in front of her work.” Teruko Yokoi’s American years After studying traditional Japanese painting in Tokyo, Yokoi traveled to the United States in the early 1950s, entering the California School of Fine Arts in San Francisco. There she encountered European and American abstraction, which opened new possibilities for her work. This shift towards abstraction is a focus of the James Fuentes Gallery presentation, “ A Pacific Line ,” which includes early works made shortly after Yokoi’s arrival in San Francisco. Her first solo exhibition in Los Angeles in 40 years, the show traces the arc of Yokoi’s career, bringing her California paintings into dialogue with pieces from the early 2000s. In 1955, Yokoi moved to New York and continued studying under Hans Hofmann and Julian Levi . With this move, Yokoi entered a milieu dominated by Abstract Expressionism. Rather than adopt the movement’s prevailing language of heroic gesture, Yokoi brought to abstraction a sensibility shaped by Japanese brushwork, calligraphy, and an understanding of nature as something experienced through both movement and stillness. Shizen – Natur, 1960 Teruko Yokoi James Fuentes June, 1989 Teruko Yokoi Hollis Taggart Yokoi’s distinctive abstraction “ Teruko Yokoi: Seasons ” at Hollis Taggart features paintings and works on paper spanning the mid-1950s through the early 2000s, including early works where her combination of abstraction with Japanese traditions is particularly clear. In The Beresford at 211 Central Park West (1955–56), Yokoi uses Indian ink and a bamboo brush to depict trees in the foreground and the imposing apartment building beyond them. The quick strokes and washes suggest an emerging abstract vocabulary. Yokoi’s work would increasingly move towards abstraction, but the world around her continued to supply an underlying structure. “Landscape became a constant throughout her life, even as she moved between Japan, the United States, and Europe,” said Wallace. “She associated landscapes with memories, and was less interested in depicting a particular place than in capturing how a place felt.” Meditation, 1976 Teruko Yokoi James Fuentes Yokoi’s later work In 1959, as her career developed, Yokoi married the American painter Sam Francis. The two lived together at the Hotel Chelsea, a hub for New York’s creative community. “During this period, she balanced her emerging artistic career with the responsibilities of caring for a newborn and living with a mercurial husband,” said Malik. “Although challenging, it was an exciting and stimulating time for her as she expanded her circle of friends, which included fellow artists such as Mark Rothko , Al Jensen , Kenzo Okada , Rakuko Naito , and Tadaaki Kuwayama .” Yokoi and Francis lived together at the Hotel Chelsea until they moved to Paris in 1961 for a year. Shortly after, they separated, and Yokoi returned briefly to Japan before relocating to Bern, Switzerland, in 1962, where she would live for the rest of her life. The move brought another transformation. In the Swiss landscape, she recognized qualities of the Japanese countryside she had known as a child, even as distance and memory altered her relationship to both places. Her paintings allowed her to bring disparate experiences together, neither wholly Eastern nor Western, but shaped by the friction and possibility of moving between them. Pfirsichblumen, 1966 Teruko Yokoi Hollis Taggart Yokoi’s years in Switzerland By this time, color and calligraphic gestures had become increasingly prominent in Yokoi’s work. In the Hollis Taggart show, pieces such as Pfirsichblumen (1966), with its energetic pink and red forms, evoke flowering without fixing blossoms into recognizable outlines. Along with Autumn Festival in the show and Spring Festival (both 1966), which will be in the gallery’s booth at the ADAA Art Fair in November, Pfirsichblumen was painted in Bern following a 1964 exhibition at the Kunsthalle Basel that included over 30 pieces by Yokoi. “These three works are great examples of how she rendered her lifelong sensitivity to nature and the changing seasons through abstraction,” said Wallace. Later paintings in the show, including Autumn light (1976), March, Diptychon (1981), and June (1989), distill seasonal impressions into shifting color, rounded forms, and carefully measured intervals. An artist whose practice moved fluidly across cultural and geographic boundaries, Yokoi resists easy categorization. These cross-country shows offer an opportunity to not only reassess her place in post-war abstraction, but also to recognize the international influences that shaped it.

title: Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize 2027 announces nominees.
summary: The Photographers’ Gallery in London and the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation have named four artists shortlisted for the 2027 Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize: Hoda Afshar , Lotus L. Kang , Sasha Kurmaz , and Salvatore Vitale. Now marking its 30th anniversary, the prize recognizes an exhibition or book that has made a significant contribution to photography in Europe over the past year. It is widely considered one of the most important international awards for contemporary photography. The winner will receive £30,000 ($40,000) when announced in April 2027, with each of the other shortlisted artists receiving £5,000 ($6,600.00). Selected work from all four will go on view at the Photographers’ Gallery in London from March 10th to June 6th, before traveling to the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation in Eschborn, near Frankfurt, from June 19th to September 26th. Afshar, an Iranian-born artist, is nominated for “Performing the Invisible” at the Musée du Quai Branly–Jacques Chirac in Paris. The exhibition, which ran from December 2025 to January 2026, centered on The Fold , a project drawing on the archive of French psychiatrist Gaëtan Gatian de Clérambault to examine colonial photography’s lasting hold on how veiled bodies are seen. Kang, a Toronto-born artist, is shortlisted for “The face of desire is loss.” The installation of suspended, light- and humidity-reactive film “skins” alongside sculptural objects is currently on view at the Bulgari Pavilion as part of the 61st Venice Biennale. Kurmaz, a Ukrainian artist, is nominated for Red Horse , an 800-page visual diary of handmade collage, photographs, and ephemera chronicling life in Ukraine since Russia's 2022 invasion, published by Éditions Images Vevey. Vitale, an Italian artist, is shortlisted for “SABOTAGE” at Photo Elysée in Lausanne, France. The exhibition, which ran from March to May, examines the hidden labor—developed through collaborations with South African freelancers—underpinning automation and the digital economy. “As we reach the 30th anniversary of the prize giving, the 2027 shortlist represents the expansiveness of photography and how it's used to explore ideas of resistance, conflict, memory and identity in our contemporary age,” said Shoair Mavlian, director of the Photographers' Gallery, who chairs the jury. “From century-old photographic archives to radical contemporary experiments, the 2027 shortlist proves how urgently photography speaks to our times,” added Anne-Marie Beckmann, director of the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation. The 2026 prize went to Rene Matić for the exhibition “AS OPPOSED TO THE TRUTH” at CCA Berlin. Past winners include Lindokuhle Sobekwa , Lebohang Kganye , Samuel Fosso , Deana Lawson , Cao Fei , Susan Meiselas , and Rineke Dijkstra .

title: How Brâncuși’s “Bird in Space” Redefined Sculpture
summary: “Simplicity is complexity resolved,” Romanian artist Constantin Brâncuși once remarked. The sculptor, painter, and photographer brought that ethos of refinement to his art. He is regarded as one of the most influential sculptors of the 20th century and a pioneer of modernism , known for sleek works in plaster, limestone, marble, polished bronze, and carved wood that emphasized elegant purity of form over detail. His Paris studio was on the famed Impasse Ronsin, a dead-end street home to a buzzing artists’ colony. The studio was the center of his creative universe: where he worked, entertained friends and clients, and displayed his groundbreaking works, whose forms challenged conventional artistic boundaries. A new exhibition, “Brâncuși: The Artist and His Studio,” at the Museum of Modern Art , traces the provocative artist’s creative life through dozens of artworks and objects from his studio. Among the most famous of these works were “Bird in Space” ( L’Oiseau dans l’espace ), a series of at least 16 sculptures the artist made between 1923 and 1940. Created in bronze and marble, each Bird in Space depicts a streamlined, vertical form that suggests flight rather than a bird itself. Three bronze versions of Brâncuși’s iconic work are included in the exhibition. In the work, Brâncuși eliminated the bird’s wings and feathers, instead elongating the swell of the body. The bird’s head and beak are reduced to a small oval plane. A radical departure from sculptural precedents that emphasized the artist’s hand and detail, the deceptively simple Bird in Space courted controversy and misunderstanding. Here’s a closer look at three surprising aspects of the work and its history. In a pivotal court case, it redefined sculpture. The Kiss, 1916 Constantin Brâncuși Philadelphia Museum of Art In legal terms, “Bird in Space” rewrote the definition of sculpture. In 1926, Brâncuși shipped a version of the work from Paris to New York City for an exhibition at the Brummer Gallery, organized by Marcel Duchamp , his close friend and advocate. U.S. law allowed artworks, including sculpture, to enter the country free of import taxes. But when Bird in Space arrived, officials refused to admit it as art. At the time, sculptures were defined as reproductions, in carving or casting, of natural objects such as the human form. Finding no such recognizable form, officials classified the work as a utilitarian object, “Kitchen Utensils and Hospital Supplies” to be specific, and imposed a duty of 40 percent of its value. The sculpture, today in the collection of the Seattle Art Museum, ended up at the center of a landmark 1928 court case, Constantin Brâncuși v. United States , in which Brâncuși defended his work as art. The case began as a question of how closely the work imitated a bird, which would clear it of the import tax, but evolved into a debate over who decides what counts as sculpture, and why. A number of art world heavyweights testified, including photographer Edward Steichen , British sculptor Jacob Epstein , and William Henry Fox , director of the Brooklyn Museum . Art critic Frank Crowninshield testified that the work did suggest a bird: “It has the suggestion of flight, it suggests grace, aspiration, vigor, coupled with speed in the spirit of strength, potency, beauty, just as a bird does. But just the name, the title, of this work, why, really, it does not mean much.” Ultimately, the court ruled in Brâncuși’s favor. The judge’s opinion in the case referenced the rise of abstraction: “a so-called new school of art, whose exponents attempt to portray abstract ideas rather than imitate natural objects.” He added, “While some difficulty might be encountered in associating it with a bird, it is nevertheless pleasing to look at and highly ornamental.” Ultimately, he decided the sculpture is a work of art, allowing it tax-free entry to the U.S. Critics see “Bird in Space” as a representation of the artist himself Self-Portrait, 1935 Constantin Brâncuși Osborne Samuel Bird in Space (white marble), 1925 Constantin Brâncuși Bruce Silverstein Gallery Brâncuși did not indulge in deep readings of his sculptures, preferring their often gleaming, highly polished surfaces to speak for themselves. “Don’t look for obscure formulas or mystery in my work. It is pure joy that I offer you,” he once proclaimed. That gave critics a tricky task when it came to interpreting Brâncuși’s work, as noted by American artist Sidney Geist in his 1984 essay “Brâncuși’s ‘Bird in Space’: A Psychological Reading.” “We see a finished, perfect product; we are in the presence of exquisite drawing and an exquisite sensibility,” Geist wrote. “Brâncuși doesn’t show his hand. He carefully gives his work titles, which seem to conceal rather more than they reveal.” In the essay, Geist avoids purely formalist interpretations of Brâncuși's work, looking instead to repeated themes and motifs as evidence of their significance. “Bird in Space,” he argues offers an oblique portrait of the artist himself, who was born in Romania but fled a difficult childhood home and traveled extensively throughout his life. “Brâncuși’s elusiveness is linked, then, to traveling, to escape, to going beyond. Bird in Space will be symbolic of his craving for, and of his flight to, the absolute.” Geist argues that the work may show no bird at all, but can instead be seen as the upright form of a man with a swelling chest, or as a phallic symbol, or even a flame. “It is symbolic of the urge for transcendence, for escape from the earthly and the contingent,” he continues. As the artist himself once declared, “All my life I have sought the essence of flight. Flight—what bliss!” Several “Bird in Space” sculptures were intended for a never-completed temple of love. Not every “Bird in Space” was meant for a gallery. After meeting Brâncuși in Paris in 1933, Yeshwant Rao Holkar, the maharaja of Indore, India, ordered three: one in bronze, one in black marble, and one in white. When his young wife died in 1937, he invited the sculptor to India to design a temple of love and peace to hold her ashes. Brâncuși’s plan was uncompromising. The structure would have no doors or windows and would be entered through an underground passage. Inside an apple-shaped chamber, a small square pool would be flanked by the three birds, at the pool’s sides. The bronze would be placed so that the midday sun lit it just once a year. Henri-Pierre Roché, the dealer who introduced the maharaja to Brâncuși, described the bronze as “struck full by the midday sun, through the circular hole in the ceiling on a particular holy day of the year.” When Brâncuși reached Indore at the end of 1937, his patron was away on a tiger hunt and beginning a new romance. After a frustrating month, Brâncuși went home. The temple was never built.

title: Sculptor Ursula von Rydingsvard dies at 84.
summary: Ursula von Rydingsvard , the artist known for her towering sculptures built from hundreds of hand-distressed cedar beams, died Tuesday, October 27th, at her home in Manhattan. She was 84. Courtney Childress , her studio manager, confirmed the death and said the cause was Alzheimer's disease. Working chiefly with standard four-by-four cedar beams, von Rydingsvard and a team of assistants marked, cut, and distressed the wood with circular saws before stacking it like bricks into enormous structures that often widened as they rose, their surfaces sometimes stained with powdered graphite. The resulting forms seemed to undulate and shift, evoking cave walls, frozen waves, and fossils. She later expanded her materials to include resin, bronze, silk, hair, and cow intestines, but the cedar works remained her signature medium. Von Rydingsvard came of age as an artist when Minimalism dominated the New York scene. She found it lacking. “There was no sexiness, and there wasn't even any humanity,” she told the artist and curator Mark Rosenthal , who organized a 2018 survey of her work at the Fabric Workshop and Museum in Philadelphia. Her work had different aims. "Her sculptural process has a great deal to do with release," the critic Michael Brenson wrote in the New York Times in 1988. “Release is one of the effects she is after.” The artist trained in welding at Columbia University, describing the process as "more frustrating than imaginable" in an interview with critic Jason Farago for Even magazine. Her classmate, the painter Michael Mulhern , introduced her to cedar, buying her a supply of four-by-four beams. von Rydingsvard took the wood to a metalworking studio and began slicing through it, looking for "forms that felt like the earth, or felt fleshy." Critics read her repeated, modular components as being in conversation with Minimalism even as her carved, organic shapes pushed back against it, and her sculptures' folds and physicality drew comparisons to the biomorphic work of Louise Bourgeois and Eva Hesse . She was born Urszula Karoliszyn in Deensen, Germany, on July 26, 1942, to Polish and Ukrainian farmers. Her father had been conscripted for labor by the Nazis, and after the war the family was held in a displaced-persons camp in Germany before emigrating to the United States in 1950 and settling in Plainville, Connecticut. There, her mother worked at a restaurant and her father worked a nearby farm and a factory job. It was, she later said, a place with “no such thing as an artist.” She helped raise her siblings and eventually worked at her mother's restaurant herself. Von Rydingsvard studied at the University of New Hampshire and the University of Miami, Coral Gables, earning a bachelor's and master's degree. She then moved to Oakland, California, with her first husband, Milton von Rydingsvard, with whom she had a daughter, Ursula Anne. She divorced him in 1973 and moved with her daughter to New York, enrolling at Columbia University, where she studied with Max Kozloff , Meyer Schapiro, and George Sugarman , earning an MFA in 1975. She supported herself and her daughter on food stamps in a Harlem apartment. Some critics saw autobiography in the work— Zakopane (1987), with its sacs of wood beneath spiky protrusions, takes its title from the Polish town where von Rydingsvard's mother was born—though she described the connection as only implicit. “I have this feeling that I have this strong link to a past that I never experienced, the peasant farmer past,” she told Farago. “Not that I want to experience it; I never asked for it. But it sort of runs through my blood, whether I want it or not.” After Columbia, she purchased a loft in SoHo, and in 1981 moved her studio to Brooklyn, where it remained for the rest of her career. She married the Nobel Prize–winning neuroscientist Paul Greengard in 1985. He died in 2019. In 2013, her 19-foot, 12,000-pound sculpture Ona —Polish for "she"—was installed beneath the oculus at Barclays Center, where it remains. “I would actually love people to touch it," she told the New York Times at its unveiling. “The acid from fingers polishes it, like the Buddhas getting their bellies rubbed.” Her sculptures were shown widely, including at Storm King Art Center and Yorkshire Sculpture Park, and entered the collections of the Museum of Modern Art , the Whitney Museum of American Art , the National Gallery of Art, The Metropolitan Museum of Art , the Detroit Institute of Arts, and Storm King. She was a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters, had been an artist in residence at the American Academy in Rome, and received a Guggenheim Fellowship, grants from the National Endowment for the Arts, and the 1997 Joan Mitchell Award. She taught at Yale, the School of Visual Arts, Fordham University, and the Pratt Institute, and has been represented for decades by Galerie Lelong . Earlier this year, the artist’s work was on view in "Ursula von Rydingsvard: States of Becoming," a 20-year retrospective at the Bruce Museum in Greenwich, Connecticut, which ran through January 2026 and traced her evolving use of wood alongside a decade-long investigation into handmade paper that began with a 2009 Dieu Donné residency. Her final gallery exhibition ran at Galerie Lelong in New York from February 19th through March 28th of this year. The exhibition included an arched, nearly 11-foot cedar sculpture introducing a new motif of upward-reaching, finger-like protrusions, first developed for a 2024 wall work on which she had traced the outline of her own hands. Reviewing the show for the Brooklyn Rail , critic Susan Harris pointed to other recent works on view, including All the Children I Never Had (2018–24), Miracle (2024), and Untitled (1995–2025), a gridded wall piece begun three decades before its completion, calling the exhibition evidence of “an unceasing fluidity and openness” in the artist's late work. Von Rydingsvard's daughter, Ursula Anne von Rydingsvard, died in 2022. She is survived by her siblings, Christine Brooks and Stash Karoliszyn, along with three grandchildren and three step-grandchildren. “They say when you get older, life gets easier,” she told Art21 in 2013. "…It does not. You know, my biggest hope is that I get more courage, I get more trust in myself, I get more faith, that I'm able to do things that I wasn't able to do before.”

title: Art Basel Qatar announces 82 exhibitors for 2027 edition.
summary: Art Basel Qatar will return to Msheireb Downtown Doha for its second edition, running January 28–30, 2027. Invitation-only preview days will take place on January 26th and 27th. The fair has announced 82 participating galleries from 37 countries and territories, each presenting a solo artist presentation under the curatorial theme “between / بين,” conceived by Iraqi curator Wassan Al-Khudhairi in collaboration with Vincenzo de Bellis, Art Basel's chief artistic officer and global director of fairs. Roughly half of the artists on view hail from the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia (MENASA) region and more than a third of participating galleries operate spaces there. Over 30 galleries are taking part in Art Basel Qatar for the first time. The fair unfolds across the M7 and Doha Design District venues, plus public sites across Msheireb Downtown Doha. “For me, the theme between / بين is a liminal space of possibility, where different perspectives, histories and ideas meet and new ways of seeing emerge,” Al-Khudhairi said in a statement. “The show explores the dynamic relationship between the MENASA [Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia] region and the wider world: how global currents have shaped the region, and, equally, how the region's artistic practices, ideas and cultural histories have shaped, and continue to shape, the world.” Regional galleries confirmed for the 2027 edition include Athr (Jeddah, Saudi Arabia), Lawrie Shabibi (Dubai), Tabari (Dubai), Hafez Gallery (Jeddah, Riyadh), al markhiya gallery (Doha), and The Third Line (Dubai), alongside first-time regional exhibitors including Efie Gallery (Dubai). International participants include Galerie Krinzinger , Matthew Marks Gallery , Mendes Wood DM , Sprüth Magers , White Cube , David Zwirner , Paula Cooper Gallery , and Gagosian . Notable solo presentations will include Gagosian showing Maurizio Cattelan , David Zwirner showing Oscar Murillo , Acquavella showing Andy Warhol , and White Cube showing Park Seo-Bo . Alongside the exhibitor announcement, Art Basel unveiled a new year-round market development initiative in Qatar. Called the “Collectors Majlis,” the invite-only pilot program is for roughly 30 to 40 new, emerging, and art-adjacent collectors. It will launch this October ahead of the fair. The program combines pre-fair masterclasses, on-site engagement during the fair, and a post-fair salon, with sessions led by Art Basel leadership and regional figures including Her Excellency Sheikha Mayassa bint Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, chairperson of Qatar Museums. “Our ambition extends well beyond the fair week: through our new year-round program, we aim to deepen collector engagement between editions and contribute to the sustained growth of the regional art market,” Noah Horowitz, CEO of Art Basel, said in a statement. Art Basel Qatar’s fair week will also anchor a broader slate of institutional programming in Doha, including the second edition of Design Doha (November 5, 2026–January 31, 2027) and the inaugural edition of the contemporary art quadrennial Rubaiya Qatar, opening November 21st. Also on view will be a survey of Giuseppe Penone at the National Museum of Qatar and an exhibition on the Baghdad Modern Art Group at Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art.

title: Rembrandt House Museum opens temporary tattoo studio in Amsterdam.
summary: The Rembrandt House Museum in Amsterdam is hosting a working tattoo studio on its premises through November 7th. “The Poor Man's Rembrandt Project,” a collaboration with tattoo artist Henk Schiffmacher and his studio Schiffmacher & Veldhoen, returns for a second run following its debut in 2023. From October 26th through November 7th, visitors can book a tattoo based on Rembrandt van Rijn ’s etchings and drawings, with prices ranging from €100 to €350 ($110 to $390) and a €50 deposit ($56) required at booking. Some walk-in slots are reserved each day. “Worldwide, more tattoos are sold than works of art to hang on your wall,” Schiffmacher said in a statement. “An old tattoo artist once called tattoos ‘the poor man's Rembrandt’: a work of art that is more affordable than a painting by one of the old masters, but no less carefully executed and selected…For us, it is an incredible honor to work in the place where Rembrandt's soul can still be felt, and to work with his etchings and drawings. Grand and small art coming together.” The museum frames the project as a dialogue between two printmaking traditions. Both etchings and tattoos begin as a drawing before being transferred with ink and needle, in Rembrandt's case onto a copper plate and sheet of paper, and in the tattoo artists’ case onto skin. Schiffmacher’s team is setting up in the museum’s modern wing, on the Jodenbreestraat site where Rembrandt and his own assistants and pupils once worked collaboratively on their art. “This is all about content,” museum director Milou Halbesma told the Art Newspaper . “We are a museum of craftsmanship, and we are trying to throw open the craft of Rembrandt and his students as widely as possible. If you translate that to today, we have a number of world-famous Amsterdam creators… And this is a chance to get a tattoo from one of these masters.” The museum also organized the giveaway of a free, full Rembrandt–based back piece, executed by a team of artists from Schiffmacher & Veldhoen in Amsterdam and St. Catharina in Antwerp. The winner, Bo Kwakernaak, a 28-year-old from Amersfoort, volunteered his back after Schiffmacher's studio put out a call on Instagram. The team of tattoo artists has spent over 20 hours in sessions, recreating Rembrandt's The Descent from the Cross (1633) across his back. The final session takes place at the museum during Museumnacht on November 7th. “I have always felt a connection with Rembrandt paintings,” Kwakernaak told the Art Newspaper. “I'm not religious, but I've always been drawn to religious imagery. Here, it is the emotion in the faces, the feeling of grief. There is a whole story in one image.” Schiffmacher says he sees the tattoo as echoing Rembrandt’s time as well. “There were so many different people in Amsterdam at the time; there would have been tattooed sailors." The finished tattoo needs roughly a year for its pigment to settle into the skin. The resident tattoo team for the two-week studio includes Schiffmacher, longtime partner Tycho Veldhoen, Morrison Cheyenne Schiffmacher, Rupa van Teylingen, Antwerp-based Frederik Moens, and Swedish artist Olof Arrevik.

title: What Sold at Art Basel Paris 2026
summary: Art Basel Paris 2026 wrapped up its fifth edition on Friday, October 23rd, two days earlier than planned, as concerns over further protests in the French capital brought an abrupt end to an otherwise buoyant week of art and dealmaking. The fair, which welcomed 211 galleries from 41 countries to the Grand Palais, announced the early closure on Thursday amid fears that demonstrations over the weekend could jeopardize visitor safety. “We deeply regret that we will not be able to welcome visitors this weekend,” Art Basel said in a statement. The decision followed widespread protests over living costs and public services, some of which had escalated into clashes and property damage the previous weekend. It left the general public with just one day to visit the fair, rather than the three originally planned. With the bulk of high-value transactions typically concentrated in the three VIP preview days, much of the week’s major business was likely already done. Still, the loss of the weekend may have been felt more acutely by smaller galleries; public days offer valuable opportunities to build relationships and introduce their program to a wider audience. “The fair started strong. Collectors showed up, sales happened, and everyone survived the questionable temperatures,” advisor Arushi Kapoor told Artsy. “Ironically, the VIPs got their art fix while students, academics, and the broader public missed out.” Indeed, while the Grand Palais was open, the mood had been markedly upbeat. The Avant Première VVIP day, now in its second year, drew a busy international crowd, with collectors appearing ready to make decisions. As Artsy reported earlier in the week, the fair got off to a flying start, with Hauser & Wirth selling works by Gerhard Richter and Georg Baselitz for around $10 million each , while other galleries including David Zwirner and White Cube also reported multimillion-dollar transactions. The caliber of works showed Paris’s growing stature as one of the art market’s most important annual fixtures. Among the most eye-catching was Amedeo Modigliani ’s Nu étendu (Lolotte) (1917), presented by Pace Di Donna Schrader Galleries with an asking price exceeding $100 million—a striking vote of confidence in the fair’s ability to attract the world’s biggest collectors—that the gallery said received strong interest. The city’s auction house sales also had a banner week, with Claude Monet ’s Iris (1924–25) fetching €50 million ($56.2 million) at Sotheby’s, setting a new auction record for a work sold in France . There was plenty to admire beyond the big-ticket sales, too. Under new director Karim Crippa, the fair featured 32 newcomers, an expanded Premise section dedicated to overlooked historical practices, and an ambitious array of presentations, several of which featured in Artsy’s selection of the best booths . Beyond the Grand Palais, there were also plenty of other fairs at Paris Art Week to peruse, such as Paris Internationale , Asia NOW, Post-Fair, and other satellite events. As our roundup of favorite works under $10,000 at the fairs showed, Paris had something for collectors across the price spectrum. There had been high expectations going into Art Basel Paris 2026, and the fair’s premature ending was an unusual conclusion. The disruption may have curtailed its public reach, but the reported sales suggest that serious buyers had already made their presence felt. Here, we round up the key transactions reported by galleries at Art Basel Paris 2026. Leading sales at Art Basel Paris 2026 In addition to the Richter and Baselitz works, Hauser & Wirth’s other sales included: A work by Mark Bradford for $4 million. George Condo ’s Woman with Designer Shirt (2026) for $2.95 million. Lucio Fontana ’s Concetto spaziale (Spatial Concept) (1961) for €1.7 million ($1.9 million). Henry Taylor ’s WTF’s my 40 acres & my mule, you lying... (2023–26) for $1 million. Alexander Calder ’s Four Dots and Brass Tail (ca. 1953) for just under $1 million. Pat Steir ’s Untitled (1992) for $900,000. Cristina Iglesias ’s Untitled (Eucalyptus Corner) (1994–97) for €500,000 ($560,000). Jenny Holzer ’s Providing (2024) and William Kentridge ’s Now Practice Heart-Work (2026) for $400,000 each. Lee Bul ’s Perdu—Silhouette VI (2026) for $290,000. Roni Horn ’s Just XX (1993) for $200,000. George Rouy ’s Unknown Lovers (2026) for £195,000 ($261,000). Five editions of Camille Henrot ’s Tristan (2026), including two for €160,000 ($179,000) each and three for €130,000 ($146,000) each. David Zwirner’s reported sales were led by a painting by Richter for $8.5 million. Other transactions included: Five paintings by Robert Ryman for $4 million, $1.25 million, $850,000, $650,000, and $850,000. A painting by Joan Mitchell for $3.8 million. A painting by Marlene Dumas for $3 million. Four paintings by Josef Albers for $3 million, $900,000, $880,000, and $600,000. A painting by Luc Tuymans for $2.4 million. A painting by On Kawara for $2 million. A sculpture by Ruth Asawa for $1.2 million. Two paintings by Elizabeth Peyton for 900,000 (currency not specified) and $850,000. A painting by Yu Nishimura for $500,000. A painting by Bridget Riley for £450,000 ($602,000). An overpainted photograph by Richter for $110,000, alongside several editions priced between $75,000 and $350,000. White Cube reported two major sales by Julie Mehretu , with Rise of the New Suprematists (2001) and Mumbaphilia (J.E.) (2018) each selling for $7.85 million. Other reported sales included: El Anatsui ’s MivEvi I (2025) for $2 million. Tracey Emin ’s You Were Part of me (2022) for £990,000 ($1.32 million). Cai Guo-Qiang ’s Bald Eagle (2023) for $700,000. Antony Gormley ’s OPEN DOUBT II (2026) for £500,000 ($668,000), and SMALL ADEPT (2025) for £250,000 ($334,000). Shao Fan ’s Giant Lingzhi 0225 (2025) for $360,000. Francis Picabia ’s Concour hippique (ca. 1932–34) for €185,000 ($207,000) and Untitled (ca. 1930) for €75,000 ($84,000). Pablo Picasso ’s Seated woman (recto); standing woman (verso) (1924) for €150,000 ($168,000). Emmi Whitehorse ’s Fish Pond (1998) for $150,000.
